scenes.title: Hook: do not drink it
scenes.retention_hook: Instant hook: the clean-looking water dripping from your AC; do not drink it

dialogue.text: That water dripping from your air conditioner looks clean. Do not drink it.
But it looks like pure water!

actions: Drops fall from the AC drain pipe into a glass
DO NOT DRINK stamp slams in

scenes.title: Part 1: where it comes from
scenes.retention_hook: Mechanism: condensation on the cold coils

dialogue.text: Part one. Where does it come from? Warm, humid air from your room touches the freezing cold coils inside the AC. The moisture turns into drops. That is called condensation. The drops run into a pan and out the drain pipe.

actions: Warm air arrows enter AC cutaway
Droplets form on blue coils and drip to pan and pipe

scenes.title: Part 2: dry air
scenes.retention_hook: New fact: the AC also dries the air

dialogue.text: Part two. The AC does not only cool the air. It also pulls moisture out of it. That makes the room dry, and dry air can irritate your skin, eyes, and throat. A comfortable range is commonly said to be thirty to fifty percent humidity.

actions: Humidity gauge needle swings from green into the red TOO DRY zone
scenes.note: Source: indoor air quality guidance (typical 30-50% range)

scenes.title: Part 3: the big mistake
scenes.retention_hook: Big mistake: sleeping in a sealed room breathing the same air

dialogue.text: Part three. The big mistake. Many room air conditioners just recirculate the air inside. In a closed bedroom, the carbon dioxide you breathe out builds up all night. Studies found more carbon dioxide in air conditioned bedrooms, and less deep sleep when bedroom ventilation is low. The fix is simple: let some fresh air in.

actions: Sleeper in a sealed bedroom; CO2 particles rise and CO2 meter climbs
Window cracks open; fresh air flows in
scenes.note: Sources: Singapore bedroom study; 2023 bedroom ventilation field study (PubMed)

scenes.title: Part 4: can you drink it
scenes.retention_hook: Payoff: why the water is not safe

dialogue.text: Part four. Can you drink it? Fresh condensate is almost like distilled water. But on its way out, it touches the coils, the drain pan, and the pipes. Dust and germs can build up there, including, in some systems, the bacteria that cause Legionnaires disease. Parts can also add metals like copper, and some coils use lead solder. So, no. Do not drink it.

actions: Water passes coils, pan and pipes; germs pop in; copper and lead tags
Big red X over the glass; Friend waters a plant
scenes.note: Sources: Slate, university extension Q&A, EPA water-quality guidance

scenes.title: Conclusion and final joke

dialogue.text: So, AC water is for the drain, not for drinking. Keep the room from getting too dry, and let fresh air in.

actions: Checklist ticks: do not drink it; keep air humid; let fresh air in
Banker tempted by free water; Guy warns him
